title: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
summary: How aHash, dHash, pHash and Meta's PDQ turn images into bit strings compared by Hamming distance, how BK-trees and multi-index hashing search them, and when learned copy descriptors like SSCD take over.
outcomes: Compute aHash, dHash and a DCT-based pHash by hand on a small grayscale image
Predict which edits (brightness, gamma, shift, flip, crop) a given perceptual hash survives and explain why
Explain the pigeonhole guarantee behind multi-index hashing and compute the per-substring search radius
Trace a BK-tree range query and explain how the triangle inequality prunes subtrees
Choose between perceptual hashes and learned copy descriptors such as SSCD for a given threat model

lessons.title: Why MD5 misses copies, and the average hash that does not

blocks.md: A photo site, a chat app or a moderation team keeps seeing the same picture again: re-uploaded, resized for a thumbnail, recompressed as JPEG, or slightly brightened. **Near-duplicate image search** means: given a new image, find stored images that are the same picture after such edits, even though their bytes differ.

The obvious tool is a cryptographic hash such as MD5 or SHA-1. As Neal Krawetz puts it in the post *Looks Like It*, comparing two such hashes tells you only two things: different hashes mean different data, and equal hashes mean the data is likely the same. Changing one pixel, or re-saving the file, gives an unrelated hash. A recompressed copy is therefore invisible to an exact-hash lookup.

A **perceptual hash** is built the other way around. It summarizes what the image *looks like* in a short bit string (for example 64 bits), so that visually similar images get bit strings that differ in only a few positions. We then compare hashes by **Hamming distance**: the number of bit positions where two equal-length bit strings differ.

blocks.caption: XOR the two hashes, then count the 1 bits. On a 64-bit hash this is two CPU instructions, which is why perceptual hashes are cheap to compare.

nodes.label:
Bit = 1 if pixel
above the mean

scenes.caption: Shrinking to 8x8 throws away high frequencies (fine detail) and keeps only coarse structure. Because the aspect ratio is ignored, a stretched or rescaled copy shrinks to nearly the same 64 pixels.
The mean of the 64 gray values is the reference point. Each pixel becomes one bit: brighter than the mean or not. This is the average hash (aHash) as Krawetz describes it.
The 64 bits are packed into one integer, read left to right, top to bottom. Two images are compared by counting differing bits, never by checking equality.

blocks.md: Let us run aHash by hand on a toy image that is already 8x8 and grayscale, so steps 1 and 2 are done. It shows a bright blob in the upper middle over a medium band. Values are brightness from 0 (black) to 255 (white). The mean of all 64 values is 100.8.

blocks.title: Average hash of an 8x8 toy image

scenes.caption: The toy image. The bright blob (up to 220) sits in rows 1 to 4; the background is darker. The mean of all 64 values is 100.8.
Outlined cells are brighter than the mean of 100.8. There are 27 of them. Note 105 in row 1: just above the mean, so a tiny change could flip it.
Each outlined cell becomes a 1 and every other cell a 0. Read row by row, the bits form the hex hash 001D3D3F1F1F0300 (row 0 is 00, row 1 is 1D, and so on).

blocks.prompt: Now brighten the whole image by adding 30 to every pixel (no value reaches 255, so nothing clips). How many of the 64 aHash bits change?
blocks.reveal: **None.** The mean also rises by exactly 30, from 100.8 to 130.8, so every comparison pixel > mean gives the same answer. The Hamming distance between the two hashes is 0, while an MD5 of the two files would share nothing.

scenes.caption: Every pixel is 30 higher. The new mean is 130.8, also 30 higher.
The same 27 cells are above the new mean, so the hash is again 001D3D3F1F1F0300. Hamming distance to the original: 0 of 64.

blocks.md: A perceptual hash is a summary you **compare**, not an identity you **look up**. Similar images give hashes at a small Hamming distance; the system decides a threshold for what counts as a match.
A perceptual hash finds copies of *the same picture*, not *pictures of the same thing*. Two different photos of the same dog get unrelated hashes. For semantic similarity you need learned embeddings.

blocks.question: Two 8-bit hashes are 10110010 and 10100110. What is their Hamming distance?
blocks.explain: XOR gives 00010100, which has two 1 bits, so the distance is 2. Only positions 3 and 5 (counting from 0 on the left) differ.

blocks.question: Why does aHash squash the image to 8x8 without keeping the aspect ratio?
options: So that the hash fits in a 64-bit integer, which is the only reason
Because grayscale conversion only works on square images
To keep high-frequency detail that distinguishes near copies
So that a resized or stretched copy reduces to nearly the same 64 pixels and therefore the same bits
blocks.explain: The shrink is what makes the hash scale-invariant: every size and aspect ratio of the same picture is crushed to the same 8x8 grid. It also discards high frequencies on purpose, the opposite of the last option.

lessons.title: Difference hash, gamma curves and a one-pixel shift

blocks.md: aHash compares every pixel with one global number, the mean. Krawetz notes that this makes it fragile under **gamma correction** or histogram changes: these remap brightness along a curve, not by adding a constant, so the mean moves relative to the pixels and some bits flip.

The **difference hash (dHash)**, suggested to Krawetz by David Oftedal and described in the post *Kind of Like That*, compares each pixel only with its right-hand neighbor. Shrink to 9 columns by 8 rows, convert to grayscale, and emit 1 when the right pixel is brighter than the left one. Nine pixels per row give 8 differences, so 8 rows give 64 bits. The ImageHash library implements exactly this as `pixels[:, 1:] > pixels[:, :-1]`.

Our toy image has only 8 columns, so it yields 7 differences per row and a **56-bit** dHash. That is a simplification for the figure; the real algorithm resizes to 9x8 to get 64 bits. The rule per bit is the same.

scenes.caption: Each cell is right pixel minus left pixel in the toy image. Blue is positive (getting brighter to the right), red is negative. The blob shows up as a rising edge then a falling edge in rows 1 to 4.
dHash keeps only the sign: 1 where the difference is positive. The red cells (rows 1 to 4, columns d4 and d5) become 0, all others 1. That is 56 bits that encode where brightness rises and falls.

blocks.prompt: Apply a gamma curve to the toy image: new = 255 x (old / 255) to the power 0.6, rounded. It brightens dark pixels more than bright ones. How many bits change in aHash, and how many in dHash?
blocks.reveal: **aHash: 6 of 64 bits flip. dHash: 0 of 56.** The curve is strictly increasing, so if a right pixel was brighter than its left neighbor it still is (rounding could only create a tie between nearly equal pixels, which did not happen here). But the curve is not a constant shift, so the mean (now 143.4) moves relative to the pixels and six pixels near the old mean cross it.

blocks.title: aHash under a gamma curve and a 1-pixel shift

scenes.caption: The toy image after gamma 0.6. Dark pixels rose a lot (40 became 84), bright ones less (220 became 233). The new mean is 143.4.
aHash of the gamma image. Outlined: the 6 bits that differ from the original hash, such as r0 c7 (145 is now above the mean). Distance 6 of 64.
Now a different edit: shift the original right by one pixel, repeating the first column. In this 8x8 grid that is 1/8 of the width, a large move. The new mean is 94.1.

aHash of the shifted image. Outlined: the 7 bits that differ from the original: five on the edges of the blob, and two in rows 5 and 6 (95 now beats the lower mean of 94.1). Distance 7 of 64: still well under a threshold of 10.

Differences of the shifted image. Column d0 is now all 0 because the repeated first column compares a pixel with its own copy. The rest is the old pattern moved one column right, and the old last column fell off the edge.
dHash bits of the shifted image. Outlined: 16 of 56 bits differ from the original: all 8 in d0 (a tie gives 0) and 8 where the falling edge moved from d4 and d5 to d5 and d6.

blocks.md: The lesson of the shift is that these hashes are tied to *positions* in the 8x8 grid. A shift of a few pixels in a full-size photo is a tiny fraction of one 8x8 cell and is mostly averaged away by the shrink; a shift of a whole cell, as here, moves the pattern and flips many bits. dHash suffers more here because every rising and falling edge moved column.

How large a distance still means "the same picture"? Krawetz's rules of thumb for 64-bit hashes: 0 means very likely the same image, around 5 means minor differences, and above 10 is probably a different picture. In a test on about 150,000 images with a cutoff of 10, aHash matched every expected copy but also about 10 times as many false positives, dHash had very few false positives, and pHash (next lesson) had none in that test but ran slowest.

Krawetz also suggests a two-stage use: a fast hash such as dHash as a filter, then a more expensive hash only for the images that pass. Most production systems keep this shape: cheap candidate generation, then careful verification.

blocks.question: Which edit leaves a dHash unchanged (ignoring rounding ties)?
options: Any strictly increasing brightness curve, such as gamma or contrast stretch
A horizontal mirror flip
Cropping 20 percent off the left side
A one-pixel shift in the 8x8 grid
blocks.explain: dHash bits depend only on which of two neighbors is brighter, and a strictly increasing curve preserves that order. A flip reverses every comparison, a crop changes which pixels land in each cell, and a whole-cell shift moves the pattern, as the figure showed with 16 flipped bits.

blocks.question: A service uses aHash with threshold 10 on 64 bits. Users complain that photos with a strong Instagram-style tone curve are missed while resized copies are found. Which change addresses the cause most directly?
options: Lower the threshold to 5
Store MD5 alongside aHash
Switch to a hash based on relative comparisons, such as dHash or pHash
Increase the hash to 16x16 pixels and keep aHash
blocks.explain: A non-linear tone curve moves pixels across the global mean, which is exactly aHash's weak point. dHash compares neighbors and pHash compares frequency coefficients, both of which tolerate such curves much better. Lowering the threshold makes misses worse, and MD5 cannot match edited copies at all.

lessons.title: pHash: hashing the low frequencies of a DCT

blocks.md: Small images keep only low frequencies, and that is why the shrink step works. pHash takes the idea further with the **discrete cosine transform (DCT)**, the transform JPEG uses. A 2D DCT rewrites an N x N image as a weighted sum of N x N cosine patterns. Coefficient (0,0), the **DC term**, measures overall brightness. Coefficient (0,v) measures horizontal variation at frequency v (stripes like fence posts), (u,0) vertical variation, and larger u and v finer detail.

blocks.caption: Unnormalized 2D DCT-II, the form scipy.fftpack.dct computes when applied along both axes (as ImageHash does). Multiplying every coefficient by the same constant does not change which ones are above the median, so the overall scale does not matter.

blocks.md: Krawetz's description of pHash: shrink to 32x32 grayscale, take the 32x32 DCT, keep the top-left 8x8 block (the lowest frequencies), compute the mean of those 64 values excluding the DC term, and set each bit by whether the coefficient is above that mean. ImageHash's `phash` differs in a detail: it thresholds the 8x8 block at its **median**, DC included. These variants produce different bits, so hashes from two libraries are not comparable.

To keep the figure small we scale everything down by 4: our 8x8 toy image, its 8x8 DCT, and the top-left **4x4** block, giving a 16-bit hash. This is exactly what ImageHash computes with `phash(image, hash_size=4, highfreq_factor=2)`; we checked the result against the library.

blocks.title: pHash on the toy: DCT, low block, median, bits

scenes.caption: The 8x8 DCT of the toy image. The DC term (25804) dwarfs everything: it is 4 x 64 x the mean of 100.8. Most energy sits in the top-left corner, as is typical for natural images.
pHash keeps only the 4x4 low-frequency block (outlined). The rest describes fine detail, which recompression and resizing disturb most.
The median of the 16 kept values is 41.5. Outlined: the 8 coefficients above it, including the DC term, which is above the median in essentially every image and so carries no information.
Bits: 1 where the coefficient beats the median. Read row by row: 1000 1000 0111 0111, or hex 8877.
The +30 brighter image. Only the DC term changed (25804 to 33484); every other coefficient is identical, because adding a constant adds only a flat pattern. Same median, same bits, distance 0.
The 1-pixel shift. The block changes (median now -422.3) and the hash becomes 9966. Outlined: the 4 of 16 bits that differ from 8877.

blocks.prompt: Before looking: a horizontal mirror flip keeps the same pixels, only reversed left to right. Will the flipped image's pHash be close to the original's?
blocks.reveal: **No.** Flipping negates every odd horizontal frequency (columns v1 and v3) of the DCT, so those coefficients change sign and many cross the median. In the toy, 8 of 16 pHash bits flip, which is what two unrelated images would give on average. aHash (26 of 64) and dHash (40 of 56) do no better. Global hashes see a mirror image as a different picture unless you also hash the flipped version.

blocks.title: Percent of bits flipped on the toy image, per edit

scenes.caption: aHash (64 bits): 0, 6, 7, 26 and 24 bits flipped. Brightness is free; gamma and a whole-cell shift cost a few bits; flips and rotations look like different images.
dHash (56-bit toy version): immune to brightness and gamma, but the whole-cell shift moved every edge (16 bits), and the flip changed most comparisons (40 of 56 bits).

pHash (16-bit toy version): 0, 2, 4, 8 and 6 bits. With only 16 bits each flip is a big percentage, so do not read too much into one toy image; on Krawetz's 150,000 images pHash was the most accurate of the three.

Simplified: one toy image, and edits applied to the 8x8 grid rather than to a full-size photo. The pattern still holds in practice: global hashes tolerate photometric edits and resizing, not geometric ones.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy.fftpack import dct

def ahash(g):           # g: 8x8 grayscale array
    return g > g.mean()

def dhash(g):           # g: 8 rows x 9 cols
    return g[:, 1:] > g[:, :-1]

def phash(g, k=8):      # g: 32x32 grayscale array
    d = dct(dct(g, axis=0), axis=1)[:k, :k]
    return d > np.median(d)   # ImageHash style

def hamming(a, b):
    return int(np.count_nonzero(a != b))
blocks.caption: The three hashes on an already shrunk grayscale array, following ImageHash's average_hash, dhash and phash. The library also does the resize with PIL before this step.

blocks.md: aHash compares pixels with the mean, dHash compares neighbors, pHash compares low-frequency DCT coefficients with their median. All three are **global**: they describe the whole frame at fixed positions, which is why resizing and tone changes are cheap to survive and crops, flips and rotations are not.

blocks.question: Why does Krawetz's pHash leave the DC term out of the mean it thresholds against?
options: Because the DC term is usually far larger than the other coefficients and would distort the average, and it only encodes overall brightness
Because the DC term is always negative
Because the DCT does not define a DC term
To make the hash 63 bits instead of 64
blocks.explain: The DC term is the flat component, the overall brightness. In the toy it is 25804 while the next largest magnitude is 3491; including it in a mean would drag the threshold upward. Krawetz quotes pHash author David Starkweather: leaving it out excludes flat color information from the hash.

blocks.question: Your service computes pHash with library X; a partner sends pHashes computed with library Y for the same images. Distances between matching pairs are around 30 of 64. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The partner's images were heavily edited
Hamming distance is undefined across libraries
pHash is random by design
Libraries differ in details such as resize filter, mean versus median and whether DC is included, so their bits are not comparable
blocks.explain: pHash is a family of variants. Krawetz uses a mean without DC, ImageHash a median with DC, and resampling filters differ too. Meta's PDQ documentation makes the same point: even one algorithm in different languages can give different hashes, so it defines conformance against the reference implementation.

lessons.title: Searching millions of hashes: BK-trees and multi-index hashing

blocks.md: A query is now: find every stored hash within Hamming distance r of the query hash. The baseline is a **linear scan**: XOR and popcount against every stored hash. Meta's PDQ documentation advises not to underestimate it for small collections, since it is easy to code and hard to get wrong. At hundreds of millions of hashes per query, it becomes the bottleneck.
Why not a hash table keyed by the hash itself? Exact lookup only finds distance 0. To find distance up to r you would have to probe every bit string within r of the query, and that number explodes:

blocks.caption: Number of 64-bit strings within Hamming distance 10 of a given one: about 1.8 x 10^11 probes per query, far more than the number of stored images.

blocks.md: How big should r be? If hashes were uniformly random bits, the chance that an unrelated 64-bit hash lands within distance 10 is $L(64,10)/2^{64} \approx 1.0 \times 10^{-8}$. Against 1 billion stored hashes that is about 10 false candidates per query, and real perceptual hashes are clumpier than random bits, so the true number is higher. This is one reason Meta's PDQ uses 256 bits: with uniform 256-bit hashes, the chance of landing within 31 is about $10^{-37}$.

**BK-trees** (Burkhard and Keller, 1973) index any metric distance. Each node stores one hash; a child hangs under the edge labeled with its distance to the parent. To search radius n from query x: compute d = distance(x, node), report the node if d <= n, and descend only into children whose edge label e satisfies d - n <= e <= d + n. The triangle inequality guarantees any skipped subtree is entirely farther than n. This is the rule in the pybktree library's `find`.

blocks.title: BK-tree over 8-bit hashes, query 10110110 with radius 1

scenes.caption: Eight 8-bit hashes, inserted one at a time from the root down. Each edge label is the child's Hamming distance to its parent; for example 01001101 differs from the root in all 8 bits.

Query 10110110, radius 1. Distance to the root is 1, so the root matches. Children are allowed only if their edge is between 1 - 1 = 0 and 1 + 1 = 2: edges 1 and 2 qualify, edge 8 is pruned without computing anything.
Left branch: 10110011 is at distance 2 (no match). Its allowed edges are 1 to 3, so we descend to 00110010 (distance 2) and then 10010010 (distance 2). No matches, but nothing could be pruned.
Middle branch: 10100110 is at distance 1, a match. Its only child hangs on edge 4, outside 0 to 2, so that whole subtree is skipped. Result: 2 matches after 5 distance computations instead of 8.

blocks.md: BK-trees help for small radii, but as the pybktree documentation notes, lookups approach O(N) as the threshold grows, because the allowed edge window covers most children. For large collections of fixed-length binary codes, **multi-index hashing (MIH)** by Norouzi, Punjani and Fleet (CVPR 2012, extended in a 2014 journal version) is the standard exact method.

MIH splits each q-bit code into m disjoint substrings and builds one ordinary hash table per substring. The key is the **pigeonhole principle**: if two codes differ in at most r bits overall, they cannot differ in more than $\lfloor r/m \rfloor$ bits in *every* substring, since then the total would be at least $m(\lfloor r/m \rfloor + 1) > r$.

blocks.caption: So it is enough to probe each substring table within the small radius floor(r/m), take the union of what comes back as candidates, and check their full distance. Nothing within r can be missed.

scenes.caption: Query: aHash of the shifted toy. Stored: aHashes of the original, the gamma copy, the mirror flip and an unrelated random hash. Each is split into four 16-bit substrings (4 hex digits); the last cell is the full distance, not yet known.

With r = 10 and m = 4, each substring table is probed within floor(10/4) = 2 bits: 1 + 16 + 120 = 137 keys per table, 548 in total. Green: substrings within 2 bits of the query's. The original and the gamma copy each hit three tables; the other two hit none.

Only the two candidates need a full check: distance 7 and 7, both within 10, so both match. The other rows show their substring and full distances for illustration (31 and 33): far beyond 10, and MIH never computed them.

blocks.md: Norouzi et al. sharpen the bound: writing r = m r' + a with r' = floor(r/m), it suffices to search a + 1 of the tables at radius r' and the rest at radius r' - 1. Meta's PDQ reference implementation uses MIH with 16 substrings of 16 bits. Its design document works through a threshold of 32, where each slot is probed within floor(32/16) = 2 bits; with the README's suggested starting threshold of 31 (next lesson), floor(31/16) = 1 bit per slot would suffice. The PDQ documentation stresses that MIH is exact, not approximate: it returns the same matches as a linear scan, only faster.

MIH is fast only when substring buckets stay small. Norouzi et al. analyze uniformly distributed codes and find a substring length of about log2 of the database size works well. Highly skewed hashes (many near-blank images with the same hash) create giant buckets. PDQ's quality score flags such featureless images so they can be filtered out.

blocks.question: With 64-bit hashes, m = 4 substrings and threshold r = 7, what is the per-substring search radius that guarantees no match within 7 is missed?
blocks.explain: floor(7/4) = 1. If all four substrings differed by 2 or more, the total would be at least 8 > 7, so some substring differs by at most 1. Using 0 could miss pairs such as 2+2+2+1; using 7 is correct but wastes thousands of probes per table.

blocks.question: In a BK-tree search with radius 2, the current node is at distance 6 from the query. Which children are visited?
options: Children on edges 4 to 8
Only children on edges 0 to 2
All children, because the node did not match
None, because the node did not match
blocks.explain: A child on edge e is at distance e from this node, so by the triangle inequality its distance to the query is at least |6 - e|. That is at most 2 only when e is between 4 and 8. Not matching the node itself does not stop the descent.

lessons.title: PDQ, learned copy detectors and building a real pipeline

blocks.md: Meta open-sourced **PDQ** in its ThreatExchange repository. The documentation spells out each letter: P for perceptual, D for its use of a DCT, Q for a quality metric. Its design document says PDQ takes its principal inspiration from pHash, then changes several steps for robustness and web scale.

scenes.caption: PDQ converts to luminance rather than a plain RGB average, and downsamples to 64x64 with two-pass tent (Jarosz) filters so that every pixel of each block contributes. That makes it more stable under small crops and shifts than picking a few pixels.
A 64x64 DCT, keeping a 16x16 block of low-to-mid frequencies that skips the DC row and column. Each bit is 1 if its coefficient beats the median, so non-degenerate hashes have exactly 128 ones.
Side outputs: a quality score from summed gradients (solid-color images score 0) and, from the same 16x16 DCT, the hashes of all 8 rotations and flips at little extra cost.

blocks.md: The PDQ documentation gives starting points rather than laws: treat distance **31 or less** (of 256) as a match, and discard hashes with quality **49 or less**. Random pairs of PDQ hashes average a distance of 128, roughly in the range 90 to 160, so 31 sits far below unrelated pairs. Rotations are covered by hashing the dihedral variants, though the README warns these are not exactly rotation-invariant.

Global hashes, PDQ included, do poorly when one image is a **crop** of another; the PDQ document lists deep crops as out of scope. ImageHash's documentation shows how fast aHash degrades with rotation on its test image: 2 bits at 1 degree, 11 at 6 degrees, 21 at 26 degrees. Large borders, overlaid text and memes also defeat them.

For those edits, systems switch to **learned descriptors**: a neural network maps each image to a vector so that copies land close together. SSCD (Pizzi et al., Meta AI, CVPR 2022) uses a ResNet-50 image network, GeM pooling (a generalized mean over the feature map, between average and max pooling) and a linear projection to a 512-dimensional, L2-normalized (unit-length) vector. Training is self-supervised (no labels) in the style of SimCLR: two augmented views of the same image must land close together, with augmentations that include crops, rotation, overlaid text, emoji, JPEG compression and mixing two images (mixup and CutMix). An entropy regularizer spreads descriptors evenly so a single distance threshold means the same thing across the space.

Because SSCD vectors are unit length, cosine similarity and Euclidean distance are tied by $\|a-b\|^2 = 2 - 2\cos(a,b)$. The SSCD README states that for the `sscd_disc_mixup` model, DISC2021 pairs with cosine similarity above 0.75 are copies with 90 percent precision, which matches a Euclidean distance below about 0.7.

blocks.title: Cosine threshold to Euclidean threshold for unit vectors

scenes.caption: At the README's suggested cosine of 0.75, the equivalent Euclidean distance is sqrt(0.5) = 0.707. Any approximate nearest neighbor index that uses L2 distance (such as FAISS) can apply the same cut.
Raising the threshold to 0.9 tightens the Euclidean radius to 0.447: fewer false matches, more missed copies. The right value depends on your data, so measure precision and recall on labeled pairs.
Cheap path: a perceptual hash and an exact Hamming index catch re-uploads, resizes, recompressions and tone edits with a few bit operations per comparison.
Robust path: a learned copy descriptor in an approximate nearest neighbor index catches crops, overlays and composites that the hash misses, at the cost of running a neural network on every image.

The SSCD paper describes copy detection as retrieval of a shortlist followed by verification, often by matching local descriptors. Both paths only propose candidates; the final decision is a separate, careful step.

blocks.md: Choose by the edits you must survive. Resizes, recompression and tone changes: a perceptual hash with Hamming search is cheap and exact. Crops, overlays, rotations and composites: a learned copy descriptor with nearest neighbor search. Either way, tune the threshold on labeled pairs from your own traffic.

blocks.question: A PDQ lookup returns a stored hash at distance 26 from the query, but the query's quality score is 20. What should the system do by default?
options: Report a confident match, since 26 is under 31
Recompute the hash at 128 bits
Treat the query hash as unreliable and not trust the match, since quality 49 or less is recommended for discarding
Rotate the image 90 degrees and try again
blocks.explain: Low quality means the image is nearly featureless (for example close to a solid color), and such hashes collide with many unrelated images. The PDQ README recommends discarding hashes with quality 49 or less, regardless of how close the distance looks.

blocks.question: A platform must catch reposts of a known image that users have cropped to a square and covered with a caption. Which approach fits best?
options: aHash with a looser threshold of 20
A learned copy descriptor such as SSCD with nearest neighbor search and verification
PDQ with all 8 dihedral hashes
SHA-256 of the decoded pixels
blocks.explain: Crops and overlays change what lands in each cell of a global hash, and PDQ's own documentation puts deep crops out of scope. Dihedral hashes only cover rotations and flips. SSCD is trained with crops and text overlays as augmentations, so copies under those edits stay close in its embedding space.

blocks.question: Why does PDQ use 256 bits where pHash uses 64?
options: 256-bit integers are faster to XOR
More bits keep unrelated images far apart even in web-scale collections, where a 64-bit hash with a useful threshold yields many chance matches
The DCT requires 256 outputs
To store the image's color histogram
blocks.explain: With 64 bits and threshold 10, uniform random hashes already give about 10 chance candidates per query in a billion images. With 256 bits and threshold 31, the random-collision rate is astronomically small; the PDQ authors call 256 bits appropriate for web scale.
